newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland mulls creating steel sector holding group.
newsitem.headline: Poland mulls creating steel sector holding group.

text.p: Poland's industry ministry on Wednesday unveiled plans to create a holding group in the country's ailing steel sector designed to help the industry raise funds for modernisation and oversee its privatisation.

Industry Minister Klemens Scierski told reporters the scheme was part of a broader scheme to save the debt-ridden sector, which also envisaged asking the European Union for a delay in an agreed lifting of import duties on steel products.

"We are considering setting up an Investment and Guarantee Fund for the steel industry," Scierski said after a meeting with top industry executives and bankers attended by Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz.

He said the fund, which could be set up within two months if all sides back the plan, would be endowed with shares in steel mills and would then help them attract about four billion zlotys ($1.5 billion) in investment needed for restructuring.
The fund would secure loans from foreign and domestic banks, help prepare commercial papers issues and seek equity investors, he said.
He said that unlike the holding group created earlier this year to consolidate Poland's oil industry, the steel group would allow the steel mills high autonomy.
Scierski said the plan could work only if the EU allowed Warsaw to extend a protection period for the industry by three years and keep duties on steel products until the end of 2000.
The European Commission has suggested that a delay in liberalising steel trade could have a negative impact on Poland's EU membership negotiations, likely to start in early 1998.
EU commissioner for external relations Hans van den Broek is scheduled to visit Warsaw in mid-October to try to settle this and other trade disputes between Poland and the union.
The final decision on whether to apply for extending the steel sector's protection period has to be made by the whole cabinet, which should discuss the issue within a month, Scierski said.
Poland's steel sector, which comprises two large plants in the cities of Katowice and Nowa Huta and many small ones, has seen sales surging on the back of economic growth that started in 1992.
But its financial results remain poor due to past debts, outmoded equipment and inefficient management inherited from the communist era.
Bankers who attended Wednesday's meeting said the sector was not fit at the moment for any new loans.

"Involvement of bigger banks in financing the steel sector is on the verge of limits. Going beyond the limit would contradict the rules of banking management," president of BIG SA bank Boguslaw Kott told reporters.

Deputy finance minister Ruszard Pazura, also present, said the government was ready to offer guarantees for selected modernisation projects but ruled out direct state subsidies for the sector. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
